### **Treatment for pMMR/MSS Colon Cancers**

**pMMR (mismatch repair proficient) or MSS (microsatellite stable)** colon cancers lack the **dMMR/MSI-H** biomarker, which means they do not respond as well to **immunotherapy** as dMMR/MSI-H tumors. Instead, their treatment is primarily based on **surgery, chemotherapy, and, in some cases, radiation therapy**.

---

#### **1. Initial Treatment: Surgery (Colectomy)**
- **Goal**: Remove the cancerous part of the colon and nearby lymph nodes.
- **Procedure**:
  - The tumor is surgically removed (colectomy).
  - The two healthy ends of the colon are reconnected (anastomosis).
  - At least **12 lymph nodes** near the tumor are removed and tested for cancer.
- **When surgery is not possible first**:
  - If the tumor is in a difficult location or the patient has other health issues, **systemic therapy (chemotherapy or immunotherapy)** may be given first.
  - For **pMMR/MSS cancers**, **chemotherapy** is the preferred systemic therapy before surgery (unlike dMMR/MSI-H cancers, which may receive immunotherapy first) [2].

---

#### **2. Chemotherapy After Surgery (Adjuvant Chemotherapy)**
Chemotherapy is **recommended after surgery** for **stage 3 colon cancers** and **some stage 2 pMMR/MSS cancers**, particularly if there is a **high risk of recurrence** [2, 15].

- **Stage 1**:
  - **Not recommended** after colectomy [2, 15].

- **Stage 2**:
  - **Not recommended** for **stage 2A and 2B dMMR/MSI-H cancers**.
  - **May be recommended** for **some stage 2 pMMR/MSS cancers**, especially if the cancer has a **high risk of recurrence** [2].
  - **Regimens**:
    - **Capecitabine** (oral chemotherapy) for **6 months**.
    - **5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) + leucovorin** for **6 months**.
    - **FOLFOX** (5-FU, leucovorin, oxaliplatin) for **6 months**.
    - **CAPEOX** (capecitabine, oxaliplatin) for **3 months** [2].

- **Stage 3**:
  - **Chemotherapy is recommended** after colectomy for **all stage 3 colon cancers** [2, 15].
  - **Preferred regimens**:
    - **CAPEOX** (3 months).
    - **FOLFOX** (6 months).
    - Other options: **Capecitabine** or **5-FU/leucovorin** [2, 15].

---
#### **3. Chemotherapy Before Surgery (Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy)**
- **Not typically used** for pMMR/MSS colon cancers unless:
  - The cancer is **advanced** (e.g., stage 4).
  - The tumor is **unresectable** (cannot be safely removed first).
  - In such cases, **chemotherapy** is given first to shrink the tumor before surgery [2].

---
#### **4. Radiation Therapy**
- **Not typically used** for colon cancer (unlike rectal cancer).
- **Exception**: May be used in **select cases** for **unresectable tumors** or to **shrink tumors before surgery** [2].

---
#### **5. Targeted Therapy (Not Routinely Used for pMMR/MSS)**
- **pMMR/MSS colon cancers** do **not** typically respond to **immunotherapy** (e.g., checkpoint inhibitors like pembrolizumab or nivolumab) because they lack the **dMMR/MSI-H** biomarker.
- **Targeted therapies** (e.g., EGFR inhibitors like cetuximab or panitumumab) are **not routinely used** for pMMR/MSS colon cancers unless **specific mutations** (e.g., **RAS wild-type**) are present, which is more common in **metastatic disease** [2].

---
#### **6. Surveillance After Treatment**
- **Follow-up testing** is done to monitor for **recurrence** or new cancers.
- **For stage 1**:
  - **Colonoscopy** 1 year after surgery.
  - If normal, repeat every **3 years**, then every **5 years** [15].

- **For stages 2 and 3**:
  - **Colonoscopy** (as above).
  - **CEA blood tests** (carcinoembryonic antigen) every **3–6 months** for **5 years**.
  - **CT scans** (chest, abdomen, pelvis) **every year for 3 years** [15].

---
### **Key Takeaways**
| **Stage** | **Surgery** | **Chemotherapy** | **Radiation** | **Immunotherapy** |
|-----------|------------|------------------|---------------|-------------------|
| **Stage 1** | Yes | **Not recommended** | Rarely | No |
| **Stage 2 (pMMR/MSS)** | Yes | **Sometimes** (high-risk cases) | Rarely | No |
| **Stage 3** | Yes | **Yes (CAPEOX, FOLFOX, etc.)** | Rarely | No |
| **Stage 4 (Metastatic)** | Sometimes | **Yes (systemic therapy)** | Sometimes | No (unless specific mutations) |

---

### **Stages of Esophageal Cancer: Definition and Distinguishing Features**

Esophageal cancer is staged using the **Tumor, Node, Metastasis (TNM) system**, which describes the **size and extent of the primary tumor (T)**, **spread to nearby lymph nodes (N)**, and **metastasis to distant organs (M)**. The **American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC)** developed this system to guide treatment and predict prognosis. Below are the **key stages** of esophageal cancer and their distinguishing features, based on the provided context.

---

## **1. Early-Stage Esophageal Cancer**
- **Definition**: Cancer is confined to the **inner lining (mucosa)** of the esophagus and has **not spread to lymph nodes or distant organs**.
- **Distinguishing Features**:
  - Tumor is **small (≤ 2 cm)** and **localized** within the esophagus.
  - **No lymph node involvement (N0)**.
  - **No distant metastasis (M0)**.
  - Often **asymptomatic** (rarely causes noticeable symptoms).
  - **Precancerous changes** (e.g., Barrett’s esophagus) may precede cancer development.
- **Example TNM Classification**:
  - **T1** (tumor invades mucosa or submucosa)
  - **N0** (no lymph node spread)
  - **M0** (no distant spread)
  - **Stage**: **Stage I** (or **Stage 0** if cancer is in situ, i.e., confined to the epithelial layer).

> **Key Point**: Early-stage esophageal cancer is **highly treatable** if detected early, often with **surgery, endoscopic therapy, or ablation** [4].

---

## **2. Locoregional or Locally Advanced Esophageal Cancer**
- **Definition**: Cancer has **invaded deeper layers of the esophagus wall** and/or **spread to nearby lymph nodes or organs in direct contact with the esophagus**.
- **Distinguishing Features**:
  - Tumor **invades beyond the mucosa** (e.g., into the **submucosa, muscularis propria, or adventitia**).
  - **Lymph node involvement (N1, N2, or N3)**.
  - **No distant metastasis (M0)**.
  - May involve **adjacent structures** (e.g., trachea, aorta, or diaphragm).
  - **Symptoms may include**:
    - Difficulty swallowing (dysphagia).
    - Weight loss.
    - Chest pain or discomfort.
- **Example TNM Classifications**:
  - **T2–T4** (tumor invades deeper layers or nearby structures).
  - **N1–N3** (1–3+ lymph nodes involved).
  - **M0** (no distant spread).
  - **Stage**: **Stage II or Stage III**, depending on tumor size and lymph node involvement.

> **Key Point**: Locally advanced cancer is **more aggressive** and often requires **combined therapies** (e.g., **chemoradiation followed by surgery**) [2, 4].

---

## **3. Metastatic Esophageal Cancer**
- **Definition**: Cancer has **spread to distant organs** (e.g., liver, lungs, bones, or distant lymph nodes).
- **Distinguishing Features**:
  - **Distant metastasis (M1)**.
  - **Poor prognosis** (5-year survival rates are low).
  - **Symptoms may include**:
    - Severe pain.
    - Jaundice (if liver is involved).
    - Shortness of breath (if lungs are involved).
- **Example TNM Classification**:
  - **T1–T4** (primary tumor size varies).
  - **N0–N3** (lymph node involvement may or may not be present).
  - **M1** (distant spread confirmed).
  - **Stage**: **Stage IV**.

> **Key Point**: Metastatic esophageal cancer is **not curable** but may be **managed with palliative therapies** (e.g., chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or radiation) to **improve quality of life** [2, 4].

---

|------------------|-----------------------------|----------------------------|--------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Stage 0**      | Tis (in situ)               | N0                         | M0                 | Cancer confined to the epithelial layer (precancerous or very early cancer).   |
| **Stage I**      | T1 (≤ 2 cm, confined)       | N0                         | M0                 | Small tumor, no spread; highly treatable.                                      |
| **Stage II**     | T2–T3 (invades deeper layers)| N0–N1                      | M0                 | Tumor invades deeper layers; possible lymph node involvement.                   |
| **Stage III**    | T3–T4 (invades nearby organs)| N1–N3                      | M0                 | Locally advanced; may involve adjacent structures or multiple lymph nodes.     |
| **Stage IV**     | Any T                       | Any N                      | M1                 | Distant metastasis (e.g., liver, lungs); poor prognosis.                       |

---
## **Additional Notes**
- **Staging is based on**:
  - **Clinical stage (c)**: Determined before treatment (via imaging, biopsy, and physical exam).
  - **Pathologic stage (p)**: Determined after surgery (examining removed tissue and lymph nodes) [1, 4].
- **HPV testing** is important for **oropharyngeal cancer** (a type of throat cancer) but is **not the primary factor** in esophageal cancer staging [1].
- **Treatment depends on stage**:
  - **Early stages (0–I)**: Surgery, endoscopic therapy, or ablation.
  - **Locally advanced (II–III)**: Chemoradiation, surgery, or immunotherapy.
  - **Metastatic (IV)**: Palliative chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or radiation [2, 4].

### **Main Diagnostic Methods and Laboratory Tests for AML**

Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is diagnosed using a combination of **medical history, physical exams, blood tests, bone marrow tests, and genetic/biomarker testing**. Below is a structured overview of the key diagnostic methods and laboratory tests used to confirm AML, based on the provided context.

---

---

## **1. Medical History and Physical Exam**
These are the **first steps** in diagnosing AML and help guide further testing.

### **Medical History**
- Review of past and current health issues, illnesses, infections, injuries, and treatments.
- Assessment of **family history** of cancer or leukemia, as relatives are **7–8 times more likely to develop CLL** if there is a family history [6].
- Discussion of symptoms, including **"B symptoms"** such as:
  - Unexplained fevers
  - Night sweats
  - Unintentional weight loss [6].

### **Physical Exam**
- Checking vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate, breathing rate, temperature).
- Assessing overall appearance and pain levels.
- Palpating (gently pressing) areas such as the **neck, armpits, belly, and groin** to check for **swollen lymph nodes, spleen, or liver** [3, 6].

---

---

## **2. Blood Tests**
Blood tests are **essential** for diagnosing AML and monitoring disease progression.

### **Complete Blood Count (CBC) with Differential**
- Measures levels of **red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells (WBCs), and platelets (PLTs)**.
- AML often causes **low counts of healthy blood cells** but may also present with a **high number of abnormal (malignant) white blood cells**.
- A **differential** counts the types of white blood cells and checks if their proportions are balanced.
- **Blasts (leukemia cells)** may be detected in the blood and reported as a percentage of cells [18, 19].

### **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**
- Measures substances in the blood to assess **kidney and liver function**.
- Includes tests for:
  - **Creatinine** (kidney function)
  - **Blood urea nitrogen (BUN)** (kidney function)
  - **Electrolytes** (nerve, muscle, and heart function)
  - **Liver function tests (LFTs)** (liver health) [18, 19].

### **Other Blood Tests**
- **Beta-2 microglobulin**: High levels may suggest **CLL is growing** (though this is more commonly associated with CLL, it can also be relevant in some AML cases) [3].
- **Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)**: Elevated levels may indicate **fast-growing tumor cells** [18, 19].

---

---

## **3. Bone Marrow Tests**
Bone marrow tests are **critical** for confirming AML and determining its subtype.

### **Bone Marrow Aspirate and Biopsy**
- **Bone marrow aspirate**: A hollow needle is used to extract **liquid bone marrow** from the **pelvis (back of the hip bone)**.
- **Bone marrow biopsy**: A wider needle removes a **small piece of bone** for analysis.
- These procedures are **bedside procedures** (not surgeries) and may involve **sedation or anesthesia** for comfort.
- Samples are reviewed by a **pathologist** (expert in blood cancers) to assess cell appearance, size, shape, and type.
- **AML diagnosis** is typically confirmed when **≥20% myeloblasts (immature white blood cells)** are found in the bone marrow or blood. However, a diagnosis is possible with **any number of blasts** if specific gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes are present [1, 7, 8, 11, 12].

### **Flow Cytometry**
- A laboratory method that uses **light-sensitive dyes** to detect, identify, and count specific cells.
- Measures cell **size, shape, and number**.
- Helps distinguish between different types of blood cancers by detecting **subtle differences** in cells.
- Often used to identify **markers on immune cells (immunophenotyping)** [1, 2].

### **Immunophenotyping**
- Uses **antibodies** to detect **white blood cell antigens (biomarkers)**.
- Certain biomarkers are **targeted in AML treatment** [1, 2].

### **Immunohistochemistry (IHC)**
- A **staining process** where chemical markers are added to cells and studied under a microscope.
- Helps determine the **immunophenotype of cells** from a biopsy or tissue sample [16, 17].

---

---

## **4. Genetic and Biomarker Testing**
Genetic testing is **essential** for determining AML subtypes, prognosis, and targeted treatment options.

### **Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH)**
- Uses **special dyes (probes)** to detect **small genetic abnormalities** in chromosomes.
- Can identify **missing or extra chromosomes**, such as the **17p deletion** in CLL (though this is more relevant to CLL, similar techniques apply to AML) [3, 4, 5].

### **Karyotyping**
- Provides a **picture of chromosomes** to detect **extra, missing, rearranged, or abnormal pieces**.
- Requires **growing cells**, so a bone marrow or blood sample is used [4, 5, 16, 17].

### **Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS)**
- Determines a **portion of a person’s DNA sequence** to identify **gene mutations**.
- Can detect mutations that other methods might miss [4, 5, 16, 17].

### **Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)**
- Makes **millions or billions of copies of DNA/RNA** for detailed analysis.
- Can detect **1 abnormal cell among 100,000 normal cells**.
- Used for **monitoring treatment response or remission** [4, 5].

### **Leukemia Predisposition Testing**
- Tests for **inherited genes** that increase leukemia risk.
- May involve **blood, saliva, or skin punch biopsy** (to avoid leukemia-altered DNA) [4, 5, 16, 17].

---

---

## **5. Imaging Tests**
Imaging tests help assess **disease spread** and **organ involvement**.

### **Diagnostic CT Scan**
- Uses **contrast agents** to highlight body tissues.
- May be used to:
  - Look for **large lymph nodes causing symptoms**.
  - Assess **cancer extent before treatment**.
- Typically performed on the **chest, abdomen, and pelvis** [3].

### **FDG-PET/CT Scan**
- Combines **PET (Positron Emission Tomography)** and **CT** to detect **leukemia outside the bone marrow (extramedullary disease)**.
- Uses a **radiotracer (FDG)** to highlight areas of high metabolic activity (e.g., inflammation, infection, or cancer) [7, 8].

### **Brain CT/MRI**
- Used if **central nervous system (CNS) involvement** is suspected (e.g., **leukemic meningitis**) [11, 12].

### **Echocardiogram**
- Uses **sound waves** to assess **heart structure and function**.
- Measures **ejection fraction** (amount of blood pumped from the heart) [7, 8].

### **Electrocardiogram (ECG/EKG)**
- Measures **electrical activity of the heart**.
- Detects **prolonged QT interval (QTc)**, which can be affected by certain treatments [7, 8].

---

---
## **6. Lumbar Puncture (Spinal Tap)**
- Used to check if **leukemia cells are in the spinal fluid** (a condition called **leukemic meningitis**).
- Involves inserting a needle into the **lower back** to remove spinal fluid for analysis [7, 8].

---
## **Summary Table: Key Diagnostic Methods for AML**
| **Category**               | **Tests/Procedures**                          | **Purpose**                                                                 |
|----------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Medical History**        | Family history, symptom review                | Identify risk factors and symptoms                                          |
| **Physical Exam**          | Vital signs, lymph node/spleen/liver palpation | Detect organ enlargement or abnormalities                                  |
| **Blood Tests**            | CBC with differential, CMP, LDH, beta-2 microglobulin | Assess blood cell counts, organ function, and tumor activity              |
| **Bone Marrow Tests**      | Aspirate, biopsy, flow cytometry, immunophenotyping, IHC | Confirm AML, assess blasts, and identify biomarkers                        |
| **Genetic Testing**        | FISH, karyotyping, NGS, PCR, predisposition testing | Determine AML subtype, prognosis, and targeted treatment options           |
| **Imaging Tests**          | CT, FDG-PET/CT, brain CT/MRI, echocardiogram, ECG | Assess disease spread and organ involvement                                |
| **Lumbar Puncture**        | Spinal tap                                    | Check for leukemia cells in spinal fluid                                    |

---
### **Key Takeaways**
- AML is diagnosed using a **combination of blood tests, bone marrow tests, genetic testing, and imaging**.
- **Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy** are **essential** for confirming AML (≥20% blasts required, though exceptions exist).
- **Flow cytometry, immunophenotyping, and genetic testing** help determine AML subtypes and guide treatment.
- **Imaging tests** (CT, PET/CT, MRI) assess disease spread and organ involvement.
- **Lumbar puncture** is used if CNS involvement is suspected.

For further details, refer to the **NCCN Guidelines for Patients: AML** and discuss results with your care team.

## **1. Screening and Initial Detection Methods**
These methods are primarily used for **early detection** in asymptomatic men or those at risk.

### **A. Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) Testing**
- **Purpose**: Measures PSA levels in blood; elevated levels may indicate prostate cancer or other prostate conditions.

  - PSA can be elevated due to benign conditions (e.g., prostatitis, BPH).

- **Purpose**: Physician manually checks for abnormalities in the prostate (e.g., lumps, enlargement).
- **Role in Diagnosis**:
  - Often used alongside PSA testing for **initial screening**.

---
---

## **3. Staging and Risk Stratification**
Staging determines the **extent of cancer spread** and guides treatment.

### **A. Cancer Staging Systems**
- **TNM System** (Tumor, Node, Metastasis):
  - **T (Tumor)**: Size and extent of the primary tumor (T1–T4).
  - **N (Node)**: Lymph node involvement (N0 = no involvement; N1 = involvement).
  - **M (Metastasis)**: Distant spread (M0 = no metastasis; M1 = metastasis).
- **Risk Groups** (Based on PSA, Gleason score, and TNM):
  - **Low-risk**: PSA <10 ng/mL, Gleason ≤6, T1–T2a.
  - **Intermediate-risk**: PSA 10–20 ng/mL, Gleason 7, T2b–T2c.
  - **High-risk**: PSA >20 ng/mL, Gleason 8–10, T3–T4 or N1/M1.

### **B. Imaging for Staging**

| **Metastatic**          | Bone scan (skeletal metastasis), CT/PET-PSMA (visceral/distant metastasis).                          |

| **Metastatic**          | Bone scan, CT, PSMA-PET/CT                                                                           | AR-V7, Decipher (prognostic), PSA (monitoring)                                           |

---
---

### **Summary of Diagnostic Pathway**
1. **Screening**: PSA + DRE → If abnormal, proceed to imaging.
2. **Detection**: mpMRI → Targeted biopsy (if suspicious) or systematic biopsy.
3. **Confirmation**: Biopsy + Gleason score → Molecular biomarkers (e.g., Decipher, AR-V7).
4. **Staging**: TNM classification + imaging (CT, bone scan, PSMA-PET).
5. **Risk Stratification**: Combines PSA, Gleason, TNM, and biomarkers to guide treatment.

*Prepared by: Public Health Officer*

Adrenal tumors, though rare, can have serious health consequences if not detected early. Recognizing symptoms and understanding hereditary risk factors are critical for timely diagnosis and treatment. Below are **five key points** from clinical guidelines to help you and your community stay informed.

---

## **1. Adrenal Tumors Can Cause Hormonal Imbalances and Physical Symptoms**
Adrenal tumors may produce excess hormones, leading to noticeable symptoms such as:
- **Weight gain**
- **Muscle weakness**
- **Pink or purple stretch marks on the skin**
- **Hormonal changes** (e.g., excess facial hair, hair loss, irregular periods, enlarged breast tissue, or shrinking testicles)
- **Nausea, vomiting, or abdominal bloating**
- **Back pain or fever**
- **Loss of appetite or unintended weight loss**

If you experience any of these symptoms, discuss them with your healthcare provider immediately. Early evaluation can lead to better outcomes.

> **Source:** [1] (page=1)

---

## **2. Most Adrenal Tumors Are Benign, But Some Can Be Cancerous**
- **Benign tumors** (non-cancerous) are the most common and often do not cause symptoms.
- **Malignant tumors** (cancerous) are rare but can spread if not detected early.
- **Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC)** is the most common type of adrenal cancer, though it affects only **1 to 2 people per 1 million** annually.

> **Source:** [3] (page=3)

---

## **3. Hereditary Conditions Increase the Risk of Adrenal Tumors**
While most adrenal tumors have no known cause, **genetic (hereditary) conditions** significantly increase risk. If you or a family member have any of the following conditions, you may be at higher risk:
- **Li-Fraumeni syndrome**
- **Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome**
- **Carney complex**
- **Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)**
- **Hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma (PGL/PCC) syndrome**
- **Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1) or type 2 (MEN 2)**
- **Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)**
- **Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (VHL)**
- **Lynch syndrome**

If you have a family history of these conditions, consult a **genetic counselor** to assess your risk.

> **Source:** [1] (page=1), [3] (page=3)

---

## **4. Imaging Tests Are Key for Early Detection**
Many adrenal tumors are discovered **incidentally** during imaging tests for unrelated conditions, such as:
- **CT (Computed Tomography) scans**
- **MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) scans**

If a tumor is found, further testing (e.g., **biochemical tests, genetic testing, or biopsy**) may be needed to determine if it is cancerous.

> **Source:** [3] (page=3), [12] (page=12)

---

## **5. NCCN Guidelines Provide Trusted Patient Resources**

🔗 **[NCCN.org/patientguidelines](https://www.nccn.org/patientguidelines)**

> **Source:** [1] (page=1), [NCCN_GUIDELINES_FOR_PATIENTS:_ADRENAL_TUMORS](https://www.nccn.org/patientguidelines)

---

## **What You Can Do**
✅ **Monitor your health** – Pay attention to unexplained symptoms, especially hormonal changes or unexplained weight fluctuations.
✅ **Know your family history** – If adrenal tumors or related hereditary conditions run in your family, discuss genetic testing with your doctor.
✅ **Get regular check-ups** – Routine imaging or blood tests may detect adrenal tumors early.
✅ **Consult a healthcare provider** – If you experience concerning symptoms, seek medical advice promptly.
✅ **Use trusted resources** – Refer to **NCCN guidelines** for reliable, up-to-date information.

---
### **Final Note**
While adrenal tumors are rare, **awareness and early detection save lives**. Share this advisory with family and friends to promote better health outcomes in your community.

For additional support, contact your local healthcare provider or a **genetic counselor** if you have concerns about hereditary risks.

# **Laboratory and Molecular Diagnostic Report for Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)**
**Prepared by: Clinical Pathologist**
**Date:** [Insert Date]
**Patient Identifier:** [Insert Patient ID]
**Referring Physician:** [Insert Physician Name]

---

## **1. Introduction**
Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a heterogeneous hematologic malignancy characterized by the clonal proliferation of myeloid blasts in the bone marrow, peripheral blood, or extramedullary sites. Accurate diagnosis and subtyping of AML are critical for risk stratification, treatment selection, and prognostic assessment. This report outlines the **laboratory and molecular diagnostic steps** required to establish an AML diagnosis and subtype, in accordance with the **NCCN Guidelines for Patients: AML** and current clinical standards.

---

## **2. Diagnostic Workup Overview**
The diagnostic evaluation of AML involves:
1. **Clinical assessment** (symptoms, physical examination, performance status).
2. **Peripheral blood and bone marrow examination** (morphology, immunophenotyping, cytogenetics, and molecular genetics).
3. **Genetic and molecular testing** (to identify driver mutations and chromosomal abnormalities).
4. **Risk stratification** (based on cytogenetic and molecular findings).

---

## **3. Step-by-Step Diagnostic Workflow**

### **3.1 Initial Laboratory Evaluation**
#### **3.1.1 Complete Blood Count (CBC) with Differential**
- **Purpose:** Identify cytopenias (anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia/leukocytosis) and circulating blasts.
- **Key Findings in AML:**
  - **Anemia** (hemoglobin <10 g/dL).
  - **Thrombocytopenia** (platelets <100 × 10⁹/L).
  - **Leukocytosis** (WBC >10 × 10⁹/L) or **leukopenia** (WBC <4 × 10⁹/L).
  - **Circulating blasts** (may be present in peripheral blood).
- **Reference:** [17, 18] (CBC abnormalities in AML)

#### **3.1.2 Peripheral Blood Smear**
- **Purpose:** Morphologic assessment of blasts and other cell lineages.
- **Key Findings:**
  - **Blasts** (≥20% of nucleated cells in bone marrow is diagnostic for AML, though exceptions exist if specific mutations are present).
  - **Auer rods** (pathognomonic for AML).
  - **Dysgranulopoiesis, dyserythropoiesis, or thrombocytopenia** (supportive of myeloid malignancy).
- **Reference:** [7, 8] (Blast morphology and AML diagnosis)

#### **3.1.3 Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)**
- **Purpose:** Assess organ function (kidneys, liver) and metabolic derangements.
- **Key Findings:**
  - **Elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)** (reflects high cell turnover).
  - **Elevated uric acid** (due to tumor lysis).
  - **Electrolyte imbalances** (e.g., hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia).
- **Reference:** [17, 18] (Metabolic abnormalities in AML)

---

### **3.2 Bone Marrow Aspiration and Biopsy**
#### **3.2.1 Bone Marrow Aspirate**
- **Purpose:** Obtain liquid marrow for morphologic, immunophenotypic, cytogenetic, and molecular analysis.
- **Procedure:**
  - Typically performed from the **posterior iliac crest** (pelvis).
  - **Sedation/anesthesia** may be used for patient comfort.
- **Key Findings:**
  - **≥20% myeloid blasts** (diagnostic threshold for AML).
  - **Dysplasia** in myeloid, erythroid, or megakaryocytic lineages.
- **Reference:** [5, 6] (Bone marrow aspirate procedure and findings)

#### **3.2.2 Bone Marrow Biopsy**
- **Purpose:** Assess marrow cellularity, architecture, and fibrosis.
- **Procedure:**
  - A **core biopsy** is obtained simultaneously with aspirate.
  - Evaluated for **marrow cellularity, blast percentage, and infiltration patterns**.
- **Key Findings:**
  - **Hypercelluar marrow** (typically >80% cellularity in AML).
  - **Fibrosis** (may be present in certain subtypes).
- **Reference:** [5, 6] (Bone marrow biopsy procedure and interpretation)

---

### **3.3 Immunophenotyping (Flow Cytometry)**
#### **3.3.1 Purpose**
- Distinguish AML from other hematologic malignancies (e.g., ALL, MDS, MPN).
- Identify **lineage commitment** (myeloid vs. monocytic vs. megakaryocytic).
- Detect **aberrant antigen expression** (e.g., CD34, CD117, HLA-DR, MPO).

#### **3.3.2 Key Immunophenotypic Markers in AML**
| **Marker**       | **Typical Expression in AML** | **Subtype Association** |
|------------------|-------------------------------|-------------------------|
| **CD34**         | Positive in ~50% of cases     | Stem cell-like phenotype |
| **CD117**        | Positive in ~80% of cases     | Myeloid lineage         |
| **HLA-DR**       | Positive in most cases        | Immature blasts         |
| **MPO**          | Positive in myeloid blasts    | Myeloperoxidase activity |
| **CD13, CD33**   | Positive in most AML          | Myeloid differentiation |
| **CD14**         | Positive in monocytic AML     | Monocytic differentiation |
| **CD41/CD61**    | Positive in megakaryocytic AML | Megakaryoblastic AML    |
| **CD7**          | Aberrant expression           | Poor prognosis          |

- **Reference:** [5, 6, 14] (Flow cytometry in AML diagnosis)

#### **3.3.3 Additional Testing**
- **Immunohistochemistry (IHC):**
  - Useful for **tissue biopsies** (e.g., extramedullary AML).
  - Markers: **MPO, lysozyme, CD34, CD117**.
- **Reference:** [14, 15] (IHC in AML subtyping)

---

### **3.4 Cytogenetic Analysis**
#### **3.4.1 Karyotyping (Conventional Cytogenetics)**
- **Purpose:** Identify **chromosomal abnormalities** that define AML subtypes.
- **Procedure:**
  - **24–48 hour culture** of bone marrow cells.
  - **G-banding** to visualize chromosomes.
- **Key Findings in AML:**
  | **Abnormality**               | **Associated Subtype**          | **Prognostic Impact** |
  |-------------------------------|---------------------------------|-----------------------|
  | **t(8;21)(q22;q21)**         | Core-binding factor AML (CBF-AML) | Favorable             |
  | **inv(16)(p13;q22) / t(16;16)** | CBF-AML                        | Favorable             |
  | **t(15;17)(q22;q12)**        | Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL) | Favorable (with ATRA) |
  | **11q23 rearrangements**      | MLL-rearranged AML             | Intermediate/Poor     |
  | **Complex karyotype** (≥3 abnormalities) | High-risk AML          | Poor                  |
  | **Monosomal karyotype**       | High-risk AML                  | Poor                  |
  | **Del(5q), del(7q), +8**      | Intermediate/Poor risk         | Variable              |

- **Reference:** [11, 12, 19] (Cytogenetic abnormalities in AML)

#### **3.4.2 Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH)**
- **Purpose:** Detect **submicroscopic abnormalities** not visible on karyotype.
- **Key FISH Probes in AML:**
  | **Probe Target**       | **Clinical Relevance** |
  |------------------------|------------------------|
  | **RUNX1::RUNX1T1**    | t(8;21) CBF-AML       |
  | **CBFB**               | inv(16)/t(16;16) CBF-AML |
  | **PML::RARA**          | t(15;17) APL          |
  | **MLL (KMT2A)**        | 11q23 rearrangements  |
  | **FLT3-ITD**           | FLT3-ITD mutation     |
  | **NPM1**               | NPM1 mutation         |
  | **TP53**               | Poor prognosis        |

- **Advantages:**
  - Faster turnaround than karyotyping (~24–48 hours).
  - Useful for **minimal residual disease (MRD) monitoring**.
- **Reference:** [11, 12] (FISH in AML diagnosis)

---

### **3.5 Molecular Genetic Testing**
#### **3.5.1 Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS)**

- **Purpose:** Detect **fusion transcripts** (e.g., PML::RARA in APL) and **MRD monitoring**.

- **Purpose:** Assess for **extramedullary disease** (e.g., leukemia cutis, CNS involvement).

  - **Echocardiogram** (LVEF assessment).
  - **MUGA scan** (alternative to echo).

### **4.1 WHO 2022 Classification of AML**
The **World Health Organization (WHO) 2022** classifies AML based on:
1. **Genetic abnormalities** (e.g., t(8;21), inv(16), PML::RARA).
2. **Myeloid differentiation** (e.g., AML with maturation, acute monocytic leukemia).
3. **Precursor lesions** (e.g., AML with MDS-related changes, therapy-related AML).
4. **Blast percentage** (≥20% in bone marrow or peripheral blood).

The diagnosis and subtyping of AML require a **multimodal approach**, integrating:

- **Immunophenotyping** (flow cytometry, IHC).
- **Cytogenetics** (karyotyping, FISH).

5. **MRD monitoring** (flow cytometry, NGS, PCR) is critical for assessing treatment response.

- **Histologic Confirmation via Biopsy:**
  - Perform a **core needle biopsy** or **fine-needle aspiration (FNA)** of the renal mass to obtain tissue for **tumor histology** [1, 2, 9].

  - Rule out **urothelial carcinoma** (arising from renal pelvis/ureter) via imaging and biopsy, as it is treated differently [1].
  - Confirm **absence of sarcomatoid features** (aggressive variant) [2].

**Key Points:**
- Biopsy is critical to confirm **papillary subtype** and guide treatment decisions.
- PRCC accounts for **~10% of RCC cases** and is the most common subtype of nccRCC [1, 2].

---

#### **2. Staging**

  - **Contrast-enhanced CT scan** of the **abdomen/pelvis** (with **chest CT** if pulmonary metastasis is suspected) to assess:

    - **T2:** Tumor >7 cm, confined to kidney.
    - **T3:** Tumor extends into major veins or perinephric fat but not beyond Gerota’s fascia.

  Infant ALL is defined as leukemia occurring in children **under 12 months of age** [1, 3, 12].

  - ALL in infants often arises from **lymphoid progenitor cells** and is associated with **genetic mutations** (e.g., rearrangements in the *MLL* gene on chromosome 11q23) [1, 3, 18].

- **Clinical Presentation**:
  - Infants may present with **non-specific symptoms** such as fever, pallor, poor feeding, irritability, or bone pain [3].
  - **Hepatosplenomegaly** (enlarged liver and spleen) and **lymphadenopathy** (swollen lymph nodes) are common [3].
  - **Central nervous system (CNS) involvement** is more frequent in infants, necessitating early evaluation and prophylaxis [3].

  - **Diagnostic Threshold**: To diagnose ALL, **≥20% lymphoblasts** must be present in the bone marrow [1, 2, 3, 12].

### **Diagnostic Summary: Evaluation of Painless Cervical Lymphadenopathy in a 28-Year-Old Patient**
**Clinical Context:** A 28-year-old patient presents with **painless cervical lymphadenopathy**, raising concern for **Hodgkin lymphoma (HL)**. The differential diagnosis includes **classic Hodgkin lymphoma (CHL)** and **nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma (NLPHL)**. This summary outlines the diagnostic steps and rationale based on **NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Hodgkin Lymphoma in Adults** and related evidence.

---

---

## **1. Initial Clinical Assessment**
### **Key Objectives:**
- Confirm the presence of lymphadenopathy and assess its characteristics.
- Evaluate for **B symptoms** (fever, night sweats, weight loss) and other systemic symptoms.
- Rule out alternative causes (e.g., infection, autoimmune disease).

### **Steps:**
1. **Detailed Medical History:**
   - **Symptom Review:** Assess for:
     - **B symptoms** (fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, unintentional weight loss >10% of body weight over 6 months).
     - **Pruritus** (itching), fatigue, or pain in lymph nodes after alcohol consumption (rare but suggestive of HL).
   - **Risk Factors:**
     - **Age:** HL peaks in **15–30 years** and **after age 55** (most common in young adults).
     - **Immunodeficiency:** HIV, autoimmune diseases, or prior organ transplant (increases risk of HL).
     - **Family History:** First-degree relatives with HL (7–8x higher risk).
   - **Exposure History:**
     - **Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV):** Associated with ~30% of CHL cases.
     - **Environmental/occupational exposures** (e.g., herbicides, solvents).

2. **Physical Examination:**
   - **Lymph Node Assessment:**
     - **Size, location, consistency** (rubbery, firm, or matted).
     - **Cervical lymphadenopathy** is the most common presentation in HL.
     - **Supraclavicular or axillary lymph nodes** may also be involved.
   - **Systemic Exam:**
     - **Spleen:** Splenomegaly (may indicate advanced disease).
     - **Liver:** Hepatomegaly (rare but possible in advanced HL).
     - **Skin:** Excoriations (from pruritus) or **erythema nodosum** (reactive condition).
     - **Neurological exam:** Rule out CNS involvement (rare in HL but possible in advanced disease).

---

---

## **2. Diagnostic Testing**
### **Key Objectives:**
- **Confirm HL** and differentiate between **CHL** and **NLPHL**.
- **Stage the disease** to guide treatment.
- **Assess prognosis** and identify high-risk features.

### **Step 1: Biopsy (Gold Standard for Diagnosis)**
**Rationale:** A **biopsy** is required to confirm HL and distinguish between CHL and NLPHL.

#### **Biopsy Methods:**
| **Method**               | **Description**                                                                 | **Rationale**                                                                 |
|--------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Excisional Biopsy**    | Removal of an **entire lymph node** for histopathological examination.          | **Preferred method** (provides sufficient tissue for accurate diagnosis).    |
| **Core Needle Biopsy**   | Uses a **wide needle** to obtain a tissue sample without removing the entire node. | Used when **excisional biopsy is not feasible** (e.g., deep lymph nodes).     |

**Key Pathological Features:**
| **Feature**               | **Classic Hodgkin Lymphoma (CHL)**                          | **Nodular Lymphocyte-Predominant Hodgkin Lymphoma (NLPHL)**                |
|---------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Cell Morphology**       | **Reed-Sternberg (RS) cells** (large, binucleated cells with prominent nucleoli). | **Popcorn cells** (lymphocyte-predominant cells, irregularly shaped nuclei). |
| **Background Infiltrate** | Mixed inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells). | Predominantly small lymphocytes and histiocytes.                            |
| **Immunophenotype**       | **CD30+, CD15+** (characteristic of CHL).                   | **CD20+, CD45+** (B-cell markers; lacks CD15/CD30).                          |

**Rationale for Differentiation:**
- **CHL** is characterized by **Reed-Sternberg cells** and is the **most common subtype** (~95% of HL cases).
- **NLPHL** is rare (~5% of HL) and has a **more indolent course** but can transform into **diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)** over time.

---

### **Step 2: Laboratory Tests**
**Rationale:** Support diagnosis, assess organ function, and identify prognostic factors.

| **Test**                          | **Purpose**                                                                                     | **Interpretation**                                                                 |
|-----------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Complete Blood Count (CBC)**    | Assess for **anemia, leukocytosis, or lymphopenia**.                                           | **Anemia** (common in advanced HL due to bone marrow involvement).                |
| **Comprehensive Metabolic Panel** | Evaluate **liver/kidney function** and **lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)**.                       | **Elevated LDH** suggests high tumor burden or rapid cell turnover.               |
| **Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)** | Non-specific marker of inflammation.                                                          | **Elevated ESR** may correlate with disease activity.                              |
| **HIV Serology**                  | Required for **primary CNS lymphoma** (though rare in this presentation).                      | **HIV-positive patients** have higher risk of HL and require specialized care.    |
| **EBV Serology**                  | Assess for **EBV exposure** (linked to ~30% of CHL cases).                                    | **EBV DNA testing** may be considered if CHL is suspected.                        |

---

### **Step 3: Imaging Studies**
**Rationale:** Determine **disease extent (staging)** and guide treatment planning.

| **Modality**       | **Purpose**                                                                                     | **Key Findings**                                                                 |
|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **CT Neck/Chest/Abdomen/Pelvis** | Assess **lymph node involvement** and **organomegaly**.                                       | **Mediastinal mass** (common in CHL), **splenomegaly**, or **hepatomegaly**.     |
| **FDG-PET/CT**     | **Most sensitive** for detecting **metabolic activity** in lymph nodes and extranodal sites.   | **High FDG uptake** in HL lesions; useful for **staging and response assessment**. |
| **MRI Brain**      | Rule out **primary CNS lymphoma** (if neurological symptoms present).                          | **Gadolinium contrast** highlights CNS lesions.                                 |
| **Ultrasound**     | Useful for **superficial lymph nodes** (e.g., cervical) or **guiding biopsies**.               | **Hypoechoic lymph nodes** with loss of fatty hilum.                            |

**Staging (Lugano Classification):**
- **Stage I:** Single lymph node region or single extralymphatic organ/site.
- **Stage II:** ≥2 lymph node regions on **same side of diaphragm**.
- **Stage III:** Lymph node regions on **both sides of diaphragm**.
- **Stage IV:** **Extranodal involvement** (e.g., liver, bone marrow, lungs).

**B Symptoms:** Presence of **fever, night sweats, or weight loss** upstages the disease (e.g., **Stage IIB**).

---

### **Step 4: Additional Tests (If Indicated)**
| **Test**                          | **Purpose**                                                                                     |
|-----------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Bone Marrow Biopsy**            | Assess for **marrow involvement** (rare in early-stage HL but may be done in advanced disease). |
| **Pulmonary Function Tests**      | If **bleomycin** (a chemotherapy agent) is planned.                                            |
| **Cardiac Evaluation**            | If **anthracycline-based chemotherapy** (e.g., doxorubicin) is considered.                     |
| **Fertility Counseling**          | Discuss **sperm/egg banking** before treatment (especially in young adults).                   |

---

---

## **3. Differential Diagnosis**
| **Condition**                     | **Key Features**                                                                               | **How to Differentiate from HL**                                                  |
|-----------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Reactive Lymphadenopathy**      | Due to **infection (EBV, CMV, toxoplasmosis) or autoimmune disease (SLE, RA)**.              | **No Reed-Sternberg cells** on biopsy; resolves with treatment of underlying cause. |
| **Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL)**    | **Painless lymphadenopathy** (e.g., follicular lymphoma, DLBCL).                              | **Lacks Reed-Sternberg cells**; immunophenotype differs (e.g., **CD20+ in NHL**). |
| **Metastatic Carcinoma**          | **Lung, breast, or head/neck cancers** may spread to cervical nodes.                          | **Biopsy shows carcinoma cells** (not HL).                                        |
| **Sarcoidosis**                   | **Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy** with non-caseating granulomas.                            | **Granulomas on biopsy**; no Reed-Sternberg cells.                                |
| **Tuberculosis (TB)**             | **Caseating granulomas** in lymph nodes (especially in endemic areas).                        | **Acid-fast bacilli on stain**; responds to anti-TB therapy.                     |
| **Kikuchi-Fujimoto Disease**      | **Necrotizing lymphadenitis** (young women, self-limited).                                    | **Histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis** on biopsy.                              |

---

---

## **4. Prognostic Factors**
**Favorable Prognosis (Early-Stage HL):**
- **Age <45 years** (younger patients respond better to treatment).
- **No B symptoms**.
- **Limited disease (Stage I–II)**.
- **Normal ESR**.
- **No bulky disease** (mediastinal mass <1/3 thoracic diameter).

**Poor Prognosis (Advanced-Stage HL):**
- **B symptoms**.
- **Extranodal involvement**.
- **Bulky disease** (mediastinal mass ≥10 cm).
- **Age >45 years**.
- **Elevated LDH**.

---
---

## **5. Next Steps & Referral**
### **Immediate Actions:**
1. **Refer to Hematology/Oncology:**
   - A **hematologist-oncologist** should review biopsy results and staging.
   - **Multidisciplinary team (MDT) discussion** (hematologist, radiologist, pathologist).
2. **Patient Counseling:**
   - Explain **diagnosis, staging, and treatment options**.
   - Discuss **fertility preservation** (if applicable).
   - Provide **NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Hodgkin Lymphoma** for patient education.
3. **Treatment Planning:**
   - **Early-stage HL (I–IIA):** Typically treated with **chemotherapy (ABVD) ± involved-site radiation therapy (ISRT)**.
   - **Advanced-stage HL (IIB–IV):** **Chemotherapy (e.g., escalated BEACOPP or ABVD) ± radiation**.
   - **NLPHL:** Often managed with **watchful waiting** or **rituximab-based therapy** (due to indolent nature).

### **Follow-Up:**
- **Repeat imaging (FDG-PET/CT)** after 2–3 cycles of chemotherapy to assess **response**.
- **Long-term surveillance** for **relapse or secondary malignancies** (e.g., breast cancer, AML).

---
---

## **6. Key Takeaways**
✅ **Diagnosis of HL requires a biopsy** (excisional preferred) to identify **Reed-Sternberg cells (CHL)** or **popcorn cells (NLPHL)**.
✅ **Staging involves CT/FDG-PET and laboratory tests** to assess disease extent.
✅ **Differentiation between CHL and NLPHL is critical** due to differences in **prognosis and treatment**.
✅ **Young adults with HL have excellent outcomes** with modern therapy (5-year survival >90% for early-stage disease).
✅ **Referral to a specialized center** is recommended for **complex cases or relapsed/refractory disease**.

### **Diagnostic Workup and Initial Staging Plan for Suspected Oropharyngeal Squamous Cell Carcinoma (OPSCC)**
*(Based on NCCN Guidelines for Patients and Clinical Practice Guidelines)*

---

## **1. Initial Clinical Evaluation**
### **Key Presenting Symptoms**
- **Persistent sore throat** (duration > 2–3 weeks despite conservative measures)
- **Dysphagia** (difficulty swallowing, particularly solids)
- **Recent voice changes** (hoarseness, vocal fatigue, or dysphonia)
- **Other red flags**:
  - Unexplained weight loss
  - Odynophagia (painful swallowing)
  - Referred otalgia (ear pain)
  - Neck mass or lymphadenopathy
  - Hemoptysis or blood in saliva

### **Physical Examination**
- **Complete head and neck exam**:
  - **Oropharyngeal inspection**: Use a **fiberoptic nasopharyngolaryngoscopy** or **laryngoscope** to visualize the oropharynx, base of tongue, tonsils, soft palate, and larynx.
  - **Palpation**: Assess for **induration, ulceration, or fixed masses** in the oropharynx, tongue, and neck.
  - **Lymph node examination**: Evaluate for **cervical lymphadenopathy** (size, mobility, fixation).
- **Dental and oral cavity assessment**: Rule out dental abscesses or mucosal lesions.
- **Neurologic exam**: Assess cranial nerves (especially **IX, X, XII**) for involvement.

---

## **2. Diagnostic Workup**
### **A. Biopsy and Histopathology**
- **Primary tumor biopsy**:
  - **Preferred method**: **Punch biopsy** or **excisional biopsy** of the visible lesion under local anesthesia.
  - **Alternative**: **Fine-needle aspiration (FNA)** of a suspicious neck mass if the primary tumor is inaccessible.
- **Histologic confirmation**:
  - **Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)** is the most common subtype in the oropharynx.
  - **p16 immunohistochemistry (IHC)** testing is **mandatory** for OPSCC to determine **HPV status** (p16-positive = HPV-related, better prognosis).

### **B. Biomarker Testing**
- **HPV testing (p16 IHC)**:
  - **Recommended for all OPSCC patients** (NCCN Guidelines).
  - **HPV-positive OPSCC** is associated with better survival and may guide treatment de-escalation in some cases.
- **Additional molecular testing (if advanced/metastatic disease)**:
  - **PD-L1 expression** (CPS ≥ 1% may qualify for **immunotherapy**).
  - **Tumor mutational burden (TMB-H)** if considering **immune checkpoint inhibitors**.
  - **EBV testing** (less common in OPSCC but may be considered in select cases).

### **C. Imaging Studies**
#### **1. Cross-Sectional Imaging for Staging**
| **Modality**               | **Purpose**                                                                 | **Notes**                                                                 |
|----------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Contrast-enhanced CT (neck/chest)** | Assess **primary tumor extent**, **lymph node involvement**, and **metastasis**. | Standard first-line imaging for OPSCC.                                   |
| **MRI (neck with contrast)**         | Better for **soft tissue contrast** (e.g., base of tongue, parapharyngeal space). | Preferred if **base of tongue involvement** is suspected.                |
| **FDG-PET/CT**                      | Detects **metastatic disease** (distant spread to lungs, bones, liver).     | Recommended for **stage III–IV disease** or if distant metastasis is suspected. |

#### **2. Additional Imaging (If Indicated)**
- **Chest CT**: To rule out **lung metastases** (common in advanced OPSCC).
- **Panoramic dental X-ray (Panorex)**: If dental extraction or radiation planning is needed.
- **Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)**: For **esophageal involvement** or **mediastinal lymph nodes**.

---

## **3. Staging (AJCC 8th Edition)**
OPSCC staging follows the **TNM system** (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) with **separate staging for HPV-positive vs. HPV-negative disease**.

### **A. Tumor (T) Staging**
| **Category** | **Definition**                                                                 |
|--------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **T1**       | Tumor ≤ 2 cm in greatest dimension.                                           |
| **T2**       | Tumor > 2 cm but ≤ 4 cm.                                                      |
| **T3**       | Tumor > 4 cm or extension to lingual surface of epiglottis.                   |
| **T4a**      | Tumor invades **larynx, extrinsic tongue muscles, medial pterygoid, hard palate, or mandible**. |
| **T4b**      | Tumor invades **lateral pterygoid, pterygoid plates, lateral nasopharynx, skull base, or encases carotid artery**. |

### **B. Node (N) Staging**
| **Category** | **Definition**                                                                 |
|--------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **N0**       | No regional lymph node metastasis.                                            |
| **N1**       | **Single ipsilateral** node ≤ 3 cm.                                           |
| **N2**       | **Single ipsilateral** node > 3 cm but ≤ 6 cm **OR** **multiple ipsilateral** nodes ≤ 6 cm. |
| **N3**       | **Any node > 6 cm** or **bilateral/contralateral** nodes.                     |

### **C. Metastasis (M) Staging**
| **Category** | **Definition**                                                                 |
|--------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **M0**       | No distant metastasis.                                                        |
| **M1**       | Distant metastasis (e.g., lung, liver, bone).                                 |

### **D. HPV Status and Prognostic Staging**
- **HPV-positive OPSCC** has a **better prognosis** and is staged separately.
- **HPV-negative OPSCC** follows standard TNM staging.

| **Stage** | **HPV-Positive OPSCC** | **HPV-Negative OPSCC** |
|-----------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **I**     | T1–T2, N0–N1, M0       | T1, N0, M0             |
| **II**    | T1–T2, N2, M0          | T2, N0, M0             |
| **III**   | T3, N0–N1, M0          | T1–T2, N1, M0          |
| **IVA**   | T4a, any N, M0         | T3, N1–N2, M0          |
| **IVB**   | T4b, any N, M0         | T4a–T4b, any N, M0     |
| **IVC**   | Any T, any N, M1       | Any T, any N, M1       |

---

## **4. Multidisciplinary Team (MDT) Referral**
- **ENT/Head & Neck Surgeon**: For biopsy, surgical evaluation, and resection planning.
- **Medical Oncologist**: For **systemic therapy** (chemotherapy, immunotherapy) in advanced disease.
- **Radiation Oncologist**: For **definitive chemoradiation** or **postoperative radiation**.
- **Pathologist**: For **HPV/p16 testing** and **molecular profiling**.
- **Dietitian/Nutritionist**: For **dysphagia management** and **nutritional support**.
- **Speech & Swallowing Therapist**: For **pre-treatment assessment** and **rehabilitation planning**.
